The cap rule allows SA 8 and SPM 8 for a soft-blocker stretch role shaped exactly like Paul's wins; both are justified by the JD's new-build and sovereign-buyer language. However, two soft gaps cap the scores: the JD explicitly requires "7+ years of experience in sales, business development, or programme acquisition within the space, aerospace or another deep-tech sector" and "solid technical understanding of space systems and their applications." Paul has 15 years in the space sector but in satellite data services (EO analytics, monitoring, vessel detection), not spacecraft platform sales or satellite manufacturing. These are sector-depth gaps within space, not hard blockers, Paul's commercial-building patterns transfer, and his institutional/ESA ecosystem knowledge is relevant, but they justify RF capped at 5 and IL capped at 4. SPM 6 reflects genuine multi-stakeholder complexity (ESA, primes, national agencies, commercial operators) but not Paul's three specific patterns. watch_list.why: Israeli climate ag tech using satellite data and AI for land-based value chains. Supply chain risk and climate adaptation framing overlap with GFW derived data product model and ASN precision use case experience.
watch_list.roast: Marvin is an Israeli startup selling a climate resilience co pilot for agriculture and land-based value chains. Satellite data, AI models, and enough buzzwords to make a VC check bounce twice. The product is a platform that tells farmers, food companies, and supply chain managers what is about to go wrong before it goes wrong, using remote sensing and climate projections to model crop risk, water stress, and yield volatility. It is legitimately useful if the buyer has enough operational complexity to act on a three month forecast. Most do not, which is why Marvin will spend the next two years teaching procurement teams the difference between a dashboard and a decision support system. You built the GFW commercial licensing program by identifying the handful of use cases where free data was structurally insufficient and a paid relationship made sense. The ASN subsea cable deal was a masterclass in finding a buyer nobody else thought to call. Marvin needs that exact skill, because their ideal customer is not the farmer. It is the food company, the insurer, or the development bank worried about smallholder loan default rates when the monsoon fails. The problem is convincing them that satellite derived risk intelligence is worth real money when half the market still thinks climate adaptation is a CSR line item. They are early stage, which means you would be building the commercial function from scratch. That is your happy place. The risk is that ag tech has a graveyard full of good ideas that could not find the budget holder willing to pay before grant funding ran out. If you can find the buyer before the runway ends, this could be the next GFW. If you cannot, it is another beautiful product that dies because nobody wanted to be the first check. Look at their careers page and decide if you want to find out which one it is.

watch_list.why: Swedish ag carbon verification using satellite imagery and blockchain. MRV credibility problem mirrors GFW open data monetization challenge. Fits EO partnership structuring skill and carbon market navigation experience.
watch_list.roast: GreenEmissions is a Swedish startup trying to make agricultural carbon credits legit by combining satellite imagery with blockchain verification. The thesis is sound. The voluntary carbon market has a credibility problem the size of a small country, and most ag offset projects rely on self reported data that would make a used car salesman blush. Satellites do not lie, blockchains do not forget, and if you can automate the measurement and reporting of soil carbon sequestration without sending a guy with a soil probe to every field in Skåne, you might actually have a business. The problem is that everyone in carbon markets has heard this pitch seventeen times in the last three years, and most of the companies making it are still trying to figure out who pays. You spent two years at GFW building a commercial licensing program on top of a free platform, which is basically the same problem GreenEmissions has except their platform is not free and their buyers are even more skeptical. The EU is tightening MRV requirements under the Carbon Removal Certification Framework, which means demand for third party verified ag credits is about to spike. But the corporate buyer, the farmer, and the credit aggregator all think someone else should pay for verification, and until you can architect a deal structure where all three contribute, you are selling a solution in search of a business model. This is exactly the kind of multi stakeholder mess you love. The ENI regulatory precedent play, the Planet three party negotiation, the AXA Climate pilot framework. You know how to find the person in the room who has budget authority even when nobody admits it exists. GreenEmissions needs that, and they need it before their seed round runs out and they pivot to selling SaaS dashboards to agronomists. If you can build the commercial engine before the carbon market collapses again, this could be real. If not, it is another climate tech good idea that could not outlive the hype cycle. Their website has a careers email. Use it or do not.

watch_list.why: UAE-based, sustainability platform, scope 1-3 measurement, emerging market footprint
watch_list.roast: A carbon accounting platform out of the UAE. Scope 1, scope 2, scope 3, all the scopes. The website promises to measure, reduce, and remove CO2 emissions, which is the same sentence every Series A climate SaaS company uses when they cannot decide whether they are selling software or selling carbon credits. You have negotiated pricing with Spire and Kpler, structured data licensing deals with Planet and ASN, and sat across the table from insurance underwriters who wanted everything for free until you made them admit they were reselling it. CarbonSifr is in a market where half the buyers do not know what they need yet and the other half are waiting for regulation to tell them. But UAE means access to sovereign wealth conversations, energy transition budgets that are real, and a geographic footprint where Western competitors are still figuring out how to spell the client names. If CarbonSifr has traction with ADNOC or any of the big regional industrial players, that is a different conversation than another carbon accounting tool trying to sell into mid-market SaaS buyers in the Bay Area. The question is whether they have revenue or whether they have a pitch deck and a very nice office in Abu Dhabi. You know the difference. If they are closing deals in markets where GFW and Planet never had line of sight, and they need someone who understands how to price data products for enterprise buyers, you should ask.

watch_list.why: E-TAC electrolyzer technology, industrial decarbonization, scaling production efficiency
watch_list.roast: Green hydrogen. The thing everyone agrees is essential and nobody can make cheap enough to matter yet. H2Pro is building a better electrolyzer using something called E-TAC, which improves efficiency and safety, and if it works at scale it might actually make hydrogen economically viable for heavy industry instead of a subsidy-dependent fantasy. You sold satellite monitoring services to oil majors who were betting hundreds of millions on offshore platforms. You know what it looks like when an industrial buyer writes a real check versus when they nod politely and ask you to come back in eighteen months. H2Pro is venture-backed and still in the prove-it phase, which means their commercial function is either evangelizing a future market or closing early adopter contracts with buyers who have P&L authority and cannot wait for the technology to be perfect. The hydrogen economy is either five years away or twenty years away depending on who you ask. If H2Pro has landed industrial off-take agreements, not MOUs, not pilots, but actual multi-year purchase commitments from steel or chemical producers, then they are ahead of the curve and the commercial hire they make now builds the next fifty deals. If they are still pitching the vision, you are too expensive and too late-stage for what they actually need. But if they are transitioning from science project to commercial operation and need someone who has moved billion-dollar off-take deals in a market that did not exist five years ago, that is your lane. You should know within one call whether they have customers or whether they have hopes.

watch_list.why: UK-based climate risk reporting for corporates using satellite EO, direct insurance and financial sector angle
watch_list.roast: UK startup selling climate risk dashboards to companies that do not want to buy climate risk dashboards. The product is satellite data wrapped in enough consultant jargon to survive an ESG committee meeting, which is the entire business model. You spent a decade at KSAT convincing oil majors they had a reputational problem big enough to pay for proactive monitoring. Map Impact is selling the same argument to every FTSE 250 firm pretending they care about Scope 3 while their CFO asks why this costs more than a spreadsheet. The founder probably has never closed a deal where the buyer was accountable for the decision, and it shows. But here is the thing. You know how to find the two people inside a large bureaucratic organization who actually do have budget authority and career risk tied to getting this right. You have done it at Shell, at Exxon, at ENI, in regulatory bodies that did not want to regulate. Map Impact has EO credibility and a plausible go-to-market wedge into financial services and insurance, which is exactly where GFW just proved there is money. If they have any commercial traction at all, you could turn this into a real revenue function. If they do not, you will know in the first conversation. London hybrid, so the commute is a problem, but the sector fit is clean.

watch_list.why: Spain/Lithuania VLEO specialist, first company launching with atmospheric-breathing propulsion, niche technical play
watch_list.roast: Spanish-Lithuanian startup launching satellites into an orbit so low they have to actively fight atmospheric drag just to stay up there. The value proposition is better imagery because you are closer to the ground, which sounds great until you remember that keeping a satellite alive at 200 km altitude costs about as much as just building a bigger lens for a normal orbit. They raised money, they have a launch scheduled, and they will absolutely get a Nature paper out of the first successful mission. What they will not get is a line of customers waiting to pay a premium for marginally better resolution when Planet and Maxar already sell daily global coverage with four-year-old technology. You have spent twenty years watching EO companies solve the wrong problem. The hard part is never the data. It is finding someone whose budget and career depend on a decision that satellite data can change. Kreios is a science experiment hunting for product-market fit, which means if they survive the first year they will realize they need someone who has actually sold satellite services to buyers who did not already want them. That is your entire resume. The office is in Spain, the technical team is in Lithuania, and the commercial function does not exist yet. You have built weirder things in harder places.

watch_list.category: AI Space Traffic Management / Space Domain Awareness
watch_list.why: Lisbon-based, just raised 15.6M EUR in Aug 2026, AI-driven STM for satellite operators and defense, growing fast
watch_list.roast: Portuguese startup that just closed 15 million euros to sell AI-powered space traffic management to satellite operators who are already flying and somehow survived this long without it. The pitch is that low Earth orbit is getting crowded and someone needs to manage conjunctions before a Starlink hits a Planet sat and creates a debris cloud that shuts down an entire orbital shell. That threat is real. The business model is not. Satellite operators do their own conjunction analysis because they do not trust anyone else to do it, and the defense customers Neuraspace is courting have their own internal STM teams with clearances and congressional funding. So the wedge here is selling to the operators who are too small to build it themselves but big enough to care, which is a narrow market that requires someone who understands what satellite operators actually pay for and how their procurement works. You negotiated AIS data contracts with three different suppliers while renegotiating pricing mid-acquisition. You know the difference between a nice-to-have dashboard and a service someone will actually put in a budget line. Neuraspace raised the round in August 2026, which means they are hiring now and the commercial team is probably two people and a pitch deck. Lisbon is not Tromso, but it is closer than San Francisco, and if they have traction with even three paying customers this could be the builder-stage role you keep looking for. If they do not, it is another PowerPoint company and you will smell it in the first call.

watch_list.why: Satellite-based MRV for soil carbon in Global South, Earthshot Prize winner, profitable while competitors burned cash
watch_list.roast: Satellite MRV for soil carbon sequestration in India and East Africa. Profitable. Let that sink in for a second. While every Silicon Valley carbon registry is burning Series B cash trying to figure out if a tree in Montana is additional, these guys are removing two million tonnes a year in Uganda and turning a profit doing it. They won the Earthshot Prize, got called out by TIME as one of the most influential climate companies, and their CEO keeps talking about serving the farmers who need carbon finance most instead of the enterprise customers who can afford the longest sales cycles. The whole pitch is built on the same Planet/Sentinel-2 imagery you sold at KSAT and licensed at GFW, except they are proving the commercial case in markets where the margin for MRV expense is basically zero. Which means if it works there, it works anywhere. You have spent a decade explaining why satellite data is worth paying for in low-margin use cases. They are actually doing it. The founder is ex-Trimble, the team knows remote sensing and agronomy, and the model works because they made it work, not because a foundation wrote a check. If you want to see what commercial discipline looks like in the satellite-for-good space, this is the case study. Downside is they are based in Silicon Valley and Gurugram, not exactly Taos adjacent. But if you are serious about finding a climate company that understands how to make satellite data pay in hard markets, you should be talking to them.

watch_list.why: Thermal imaging constellation for agriculture and water monitoring, raised $20M+ and filling gap Planet cannot address
watch_list.roast: Thermal infrared from space for precision agriculture, water stress monitoring, and industrial heat leak detection. They are building a constellation of smallsats to image surface temperature at field scale, which is the one thing Planet cannot give you and the thing every agronomist actually wants when they say they want satellite data. The use case is obvious, the tech is hard, and the customer base is real. Insurance, agriculture, utilities, anyone trying to price water risk or optimize irrigation at scale. You have sold satellite data to oil majors who did not know they needed it, you have licensed EO to conservation buyers who could not afford it, and you have built partnerships with people who had no idea how to use imagery until you showed them. Hydrosat has a cleaner value prop than any of that. Their problem is not explaining why thermal matters. Their problem is scaling the constellation, keeping the refresh rate high enough to matter, and making sure the data gets into the hands of the decision makers instead of stopping at the agtech middleware layer that takes the margin and adds the jargon. The team is ex-NASA JPL and ex-Planet, so they know how to build the hardware and they know how to talk to the commercial market. They raised a Series A from Finistere and Energy Innovation Capital, which tells you the ag and climate infrastructure money is taking them seriously. If you are looking for an EO company where the satellite is the hard part and the commercial argument is the easy part, instead of the other way around, this is that company. Based in Luxembourg and DC, so the commute is a problem, but the job is real.

watch_list.why: YC-backed electric cargo ship startup with $100M+ in sales, first commercial deployment 2026, MIT battery tech and experienced maritime founders
watch_list.roast: Electric cargo ships. Not a study, not a pilot, not a render on a pitch deck. Actual sales contracts, over one hundred million dollars, first vessel deploying in early 2026, backed by the largest maritime VC in the world. The founders previously started two shipping lines, so they know what breaks and what sells, and the battery and solar stack is a spinout from MIT Ocean Engineering, so the tech is not vaporware. They claim four times the profitability of diesel vessels, which if true means the green premium is negative and the adoption curve is a question of production capacity, not buyer conversion. You spent a decade selling to offshore energy companies and ship operators. You know exactly how conservative that buyer base is and exactly how hard it is to move them off the technology that works. If Voltic has real contracts from real shipping companies, that means they solved the financing conversation, the safety conversation, the route economics conversation, and the regulatory conversation. All of which are harder than the technology conversation. The YC batch gives them access to growth capital and the maritime VC backing gives them access to shipyard relationships and flag state credibility. The business model is Crushing As A Service for the ocean. Lease the ship, capture the fuel savings, prove the unit economics, then scale the fleet. If it works, it is the next Maersk. If it does not, it is another electric vehicle company that could not get past the prototype. But the contracts suggest it works. You should talk to them before they hire someone else who has never sold a satellite service to an oil major and does not know how to negotiate a multi-year master agreement with a procurement team that moves like a glacier. Based in the US, so no Tromso nostalgia, but the mission is decarbonizing the hardest sector and the team has done it before.

watch_list.why: Digital MRV platform using satellite + AI, farmer-focused carbon forward contracts, fits Paul's GFW partnership model and EO licensing background
watch_list.roast: Earthbanc sells farmer reforestation credits with a digital MRV app and satellite remote sensing stack. They claim to automate carbon project development and finance. Noble mission. The problem is that you have seen this movie before, twice, and you know how it ends. At GFW you spent three years explaining to buyers that free data does not mean no value, that the commercial argument lives in the relationship not the raster. At KSAT you carried oil spill monitoring proposals to six continents before anyone signed. Earthbanc is at the part of the arc where the technology works and the financing model makes sense on a whiteboard and the founders believe that the market will meet them halfway. It will not. Someone has to build the buyer relationships one pipeline call at a time. You are that someone. The company needs a commercial operator who knows the difference between a working MRV stack and a revenue model, who has closed deals with insurance companies and conservation buyers, and who will not flinch when the pilot customer asks for another six months of free data before committing. You have done all of this. The question is whether you want to do it again in a different accent with farmers in the tropics instead of fishing boats in the Southern Ocean. If the answer is yes, this is the call you make. If the answer is no, skip it. But do not pretend the fit is unclear.

watch_list.why: Enhanced rock weathering MRV platform, emerging carbon removal pathway, fits Paul's technical credibility with novel EO applications (ASN subsea parallel)
watch_list.roast: CREW Carbon builds MRV infrastructure for enhanced rock weathering, which is the carbon removal pathway that sounds like a geology term paper until you realize it might actually scale. Spread crushed basalt on farmland, it weathers faster, pulls CO2 out of the air, you measure it, you sell credits. CREW provides the measurement layer. The company is early, the removal method is not proven at scale, and the number of corporate buyers who wake up in the morning excited to finance rock spreading in Iowa is currently a rounding error. This is either the next legitimate carbon removal vertical or it is enhanced oil recovery for the ESG set. You will not know which until someone tries to sell it. That should be you. You have the combination of technical credibility and commercial instinct that this kind of nascent market requires. You sold oil spill monitoring before oil spill monitoring was a category. You turned ASN subsea cable protection into a use case that did not exist eighteen months prior. You know how to find the buyer who has a problem they do not yet know they have and convince them that your client has the answer. CREW Carbon needs that skill badly. The question is whether you want to spend the next two years explaining enhanced weathering to carbon credit brokers and agricultural co-ops or whether you would rather work in a market that already has definitions. Both are legitimate answers. Only one of them is this job.

watch_list.why: YC-backed, satellite water risk platform, Coca-Cola/Diageo/AbInBev customers
watch_list.roast: Waterplan combines corporate operational data with local water satellite imagery to give you a continuously updated financial assessment of water risk, which is a polite way of saying they built the dashboard that tells Coca-Cola exactly how screwed their bottling plants are when the aquifer runs dry in three years instead of five. The customer list is genuinely impressive, Diageo and Colgate and AB InBev, which means someone in procurement finally got tired of the quarterly risk report that said everything was fine until the day the wells went dry. The platform offers tailored mitigation opportunities from conventional infrastructure to nature-based solutions, which covers the range from we should probably build a reservoir to maybe plant some trees and hope. Paul has spent two decades in the space where satellite data becomes a commercial argument, and Waterplan is exactly that argument aimed at the one thing every industrial operation actually worries about when the ESG presentation is over. The product is defensible, the buyer has budget, and the regulatory pressure is only getting louder. The YC pedigree means they raised fast and probably burned faster, but if the customer list is real and renewing, the commercial model works. The question is whether they need someone who can build the go-to-market function from scratch or whether they already have twelve account executives in Austin and just need another one. Either way, Paul has sold satellite-derived risk products to oil majors and insurance carriers, and water risk is the same sale with a different slide deck and a better narrative.

watch_list.why: 10cm resolution commercial optical launching 2026, climate/defense dual-use
watch_list.roast: Albedo is building the first commercial satellite that can actually read license plates from space, which sounds incredible until you remember that means everyone with a credit card can also read license plates from space. They raised $60M to put 10cm optical resolution into low orbit, which is the kind of thing that makes defense buyers salivate and privacy advocates reach for the Xanax. The founder pitch is that climate monitoring and infrastructure inspection need this resolution, which is true, but the actual buyer list is going to be 80% three-letter agencies and 20% very paranoid insurance companies. Paul spent a decade at KSAT convincing oil majors that they needed to know where their rigs were leaking before Greenpeace did. Albedo is the same game, different altitude. The technical risk is orbital mechanics at very low altitude, the commercial risk is that they become a political football before they hit profitability, and the opportunity is that if the first bird works, they have no competition for two years. Worth a conversation, but prepare to explain how you feel about selling imagery to people who already have too much imagery.

watch_list.why: Thermal constellation for wildfire early detection, EU/US market, Munich-based
watch_list.roast: OroraTech is a German startup that put thermal cameras in orbit to catch wildfires before they turn into apocalypses, which is a genuinely useful idea in a world where California and Australia burn every summer like clockwork. They have a working constellation, actual customers in forestry and insurance, and backing from the EU climate apparatus, which sounds great until you realize their go-to-market is having to explain to fire agencies why satellite detection is better than the veteran ranger who has been watching the ridgeline for thirty years. Paul has sold satellite monitoring to organizations that did not think they needed satellite monitoring. Shell did not wake up one day and decide they needed weekly radar sweeps of the North Sea. Paul built that need one spill report at a time. OroraTech has the same structure: the value is obvious in hindsight, invisible in foresight, and the commercial path is convincing buyers before the catastrophe instead of after it. They are Munich-based with some US expansion talk, which is either an exciting internationalization play or a time zone nightmare depending on how much Paul wants to spend his mornings on calls with Bavaria. The wildfire market is real, the insurance vertical is mature, the regulatory pressure is rising. If they have budget for someone who can speak both satellite and commercial without needing a translator, Paul should be on that shortlist.

watch_list.why: UK-based, won EU EUDR contract for forest history data, satellite-based forest carbon MRV, direct EO-to-carbon market link
watch_list.roast: Space Intelligence is what happens when you take the carbon credit credibility crisis seriously and decide satellites might actually solve it instead of making it worse. They won the EU deforestation regulation contract, which means they get to tell importers whether their coffee came from a forest that existed last year or a parking lot that used to be a forest. The business model is MRV for people who got burned by REDD+ promises in 2015 and want someone else to hold the liability when Greenpeace comes asking questions. You spent a decade at KSAT selling oil spill monitoring to guys who did not want to be monitored. This is the same structural tension but the customer actually wants to be caught doing the right thing for once. Edinburgh office, which means you would be explaining the value of 10-meter SAR to procurement people in Brussels who think high resolution means they can see individual trees. If you can sell EMSA on proactive monitoring when they had no budget, you can sell DG Environment on forest baselines when they have a mandate. The UK climate tech scene has gotten serious in the last two years. This one has revenue, a regulatory tailwind, and a product the market has to buy whether or not it wants to. That is rarer than it should be.

watch_list.why: Lens platform, partners with Space Intelligence, data access layer for EO-to-enterprise, California-based, selling infrastructure not insights
watch_list.roast: Upstream Tech is doing the boring thing nobody wants to fund and everybody needs, which is building the data plumbing so that satellite imagery does not sit in a STAC catalog being technically accessible and functionally useless. The Lens platform is Snowflake for people who know what a shapefile is. They just partnered with Space Intelligence to make forest monitoring data not require a PhD to query, which tells you the market has matured past the part where having a data scientist on staff was a differentiator and into the part where enterprise customers want an API and a invoice. You built the first iteration of this at GFW when you realized nobody outside of three people could actually use the data portal you shipped. The difference here is they are selling it instead of giving it away and then wondering why the pipeline is too narrow. This is infrastructure in the least sexy sense, which in 2026 is where the money actually is. They are California-based, raised a Series A, and are downstream of every satellite operator with a marginal cost problem. If you can explain why Planet imagery is worth 90 percent off list when structured into a partnership, you can explain why Lens is worth sixty grand a seat when it means six months of analyst time gets compressed into six hours of queries. The GTM motion is sell once to the data provider, monetize forever from the enterprise customer who was never going to build this themselves. You have done both sides of that deal.

watch_list.why: Australia-based, tour operator vertical, workflow automation plus carbon reporting, niche enough to own, big enough to matter
watch_list.roast: Dazhboards went full vertical SaaS on the tourism industry and decided carbon accounting was the wedge to get tour operators to care about workflow automation, which is either brilliant or six months from a pivot depending on whether you think tourism operators in Queensland give a damn about Scope 3 emissions reporting. The product automates booking, scheduling, and invoicing and then calculates carbon per tour as a feature instead of the reason you bought it, which is the only way this works because nobody wakes up wanting to measure their footprint but everybody wants their invoicing to not be a Google Sheet. This is the insurance vertical play you tried at GFW with AXA and QBE but instead of selling climate risk they are selling operational efficiency and giving away the carbon data as a trust signal. Australia has gotten weird about sustainability disclosure in the last 18 months and the tour industry has enough margin to pay for software but not enough to hire a consultant. If you can close an ASN subsea cable deal by identifying a non-obvious application for vessel tracking data, you can close a sustainability SaaS deal by explaining that the carbon output is what gets them the next round of regional tourism grants. This is too small for Salesforce to care about and too workflow-specific for a generalist to win. You have sold into weird verticals before. This one has product-market fit and a regulatory tailwind they did not have to create themselves. Sydney or remote.

watch_list.why: Madrid-based, $130M Series B (April 2026), selling enterprise access to real-time geospatial intel for supply chains, ag, insurance, urban planning. Multi-stakeholder EO platform play.
watch_list.roast: So a Spanish startup just raised $130 million to become the Snowflake of satellite data and you are sitting in Taos refreshing LinkedIn. Xoople is doing the thing you spent a decade building at KSAT and three years attempting at GFW, except they convinced Nazca Capital and a consortium of European money that the geospatial data infrastructure layer is actually worth owning. They are selling the same enterprise buyer the same story you have been telling since the ENI days, the one where supply chain visibility and parametric insurance become unteachable without live Earth observation feeds, except they are in Madrid and you are in New Mexico waiting for the phone to ring. Their customer list reads like your Rolodex if your Rolodex had followed through. The company is Series B, which means they have already survived the part where you have to convince a room full of people that this is a real business and not just a science project with a revenue hypothesis. You have closed harder deals with worse odds. This one you could probably close in your sleep, assuming they are hiring and you are willing to explain to your son why you are learning Spanish in your fifties.

watch_list.why: India-based SAR specialist, part of public-private consortium building India's first EO constellation. Series A stage, maritime and foliage penetration focus. Emerging market, tough domain.
watch_list.roast: PierSight is the SAR specialist inside the Indian government consortium building the country's first serious Earth observation constellation and you are going to scroll right past it because it is in India and you have never worked in India and maybe this is not the right time to learn. Except the entire thesis of your career has been showing up early to markets where the regulatory environment is changing faster than the commercial infrastructure can keep up, and India in 2026 is exactly that market at exactly that moment. They are in Series A, which means they have government contracts and technical credibility but they probably do not have a person who has spent a decade selling SAR-derived intelligence to offshore energy companies and insurers who will only buy if you can make the case in the language of risk transfer and regulatory compliance. You made that case to ENI, to Shell, to the Australians when NOPSEMA was still figuring out what proactive monitoring even meant. PierSight has the constellation and the public-private tailwind and a maritime surveillance product that needs someone who knows how to sell the thing before the data exists. The location is hard, the time zone is worse, but if you are seriously looking for a place where you can build a commercial function from scratch in a domain you already own, this is that place. You would just have to be willing to get on a plane.

watch_list.category: AI-Powered Carbon MRV / Satellite Remote Sensing
watch_list.why: AI-based MRV using satellite imagery and ML for nature-based carbon credits, direct overlap with GFW satellite data licensing and Planet deal experience
watch_list.roast: Indian startup processing satellite imagery through machine learning to verify carbon credits and automate MRV reporting. Blockchain ledger, real-time insights, the full stack. You have spent a decade explaining to people that high-latency conservation detection is not a threat to commercial intelligence because the use cases are structurally different. You closed a 1.2 billion hectare Planet deal by understanding that distinction cold. VANYA is selling the same structural argument but in carbon markets instead of maritime. The buyers are different but the objection is identical. Someone needs to go in there and tell them which carbon registries will actually pay for automated MRV and which ones are still married to manual audits because the methodology lets them charge more. The opportunity is not the technology. The technology works. The opportunity is figuring out who has budget authority at Verra and Gold Standard and whether the pilot-to-precedent engine runs the same way in carbon markets as it did in offshore oil regulation. If it does, you already know this movie. If it does not, you will figure that out in the first three phone calls. Either way, you have done harder.

watch_list.category: Full-Stack Carbon Removal Platform / Regenerative Agriculture MRV
watch_list.why: Combines AI, blockchain, satellite tech, and digital MRV for smallholder farmer carbon markets, direct parallel to GFW's mission-commercial tension and multi-stakeholder ecosystem work
watch_list.roast: Full-stack carbon removal platform for smallholder farmers using AI, blockchain, satellite intelligence, and digital MRV. The pitch is that they let farmers in the Global South participate in voluntary carbon markets while generating measurable impact. The complexity is not the sensing. The complexity is assembling a value chain where the farmer gets paid, the carbon buyer trusts the credit, the registry accepts the methodology, and nobody walks away when the first verification audit costs more than the first ton sold. You spent two years at GFW building a commercial licensing program on top of a platform designed to give everything away for free. You know what it feels like when the internal logic of the organization and the external logic of the market are not naturally aligned and you have to build the bridge yourself. Prithu has that same problem but in a different shape. The mission is farmers. The revenue is corporate carbon buyers. The infrastructure is satellite MRV. You have sold satellite data to insurance companies who needed parametric risk framing and you have sold it to NGOs who needed impact measurement and you have sold it to oil majors who needed regulatory compliance. This is all three at once. If that does not make you interested, nothing will.

watch_list.category: Agroforestry & Reforestation MRV / Satellite + Field Sensors
watch_list.why: Comprehensive MRV for agroforestry combining satellite monitoring, field sensors, mobile apps, socioeconomic metrics alongside carbon, Amsterdam-based with holistic project performance measurement
watch_list.roast: Amsterdam-based MRV system for agroforestry and reforestation combining satellite monitoring, field sensors, and mobile apps for continuous verification. They track carbon sequestration, biodiversity, water benefits, and community economic outcomes in one integrated platform. Holistic view, socioeconomic metrics, the whole responsible capitalism performance dashboard. You negotiated a three-party Planet deal where the objection was competitive harm and the resolution was structural use-case separation. You built an ASN partnership by identifying a non-obvious application for GFW data in subsea infrastructure. You know how to find the stakeholder map and figure out who actually controls the decision even when the org chart says someone else. Treecycle is selling MRV as a service but the real product is trust infrastructure for agroforestry projects that need to prove impact to different audiences at the same time. Farmers need proof for subsidy programs. NGOs need proof for grants. Carbon buyers need proof for offsets. One data stack, three different commercial arguments. That is not a technology problem. That is a BD problem. The question is whether the European agroforestry market is mature enough to pay for this or whether you spend two years doing pilot projects for co-benefit storytelling and then discover the margin is in selling the software to someone else. If you can answer that question in the first month, the role is worth it. If you cannot, it is just another undercapitalized climate tech company with good sensors and no GTM.

watch_list.why: On-truck carbon capture devices for heavy transport, $117M funded, real deployed units, direct fit with Paul's commercial structuring and multi-stakeholder deal experience
watch_list.roast: Remora bolts a carbon capture device to the back of a semi truck, pulls CO2 out of diesel exhaust, and sells the captured carbon as feedstock or for sequestration. They have raised $117 million, which means someone believes this works at scale or at least believes someone else will believe it by the time the Series B closes. The technology is genuinely interesting. Diesel combustion is a point source you can access without building new infrastructure, the unit economics depend on whether fleet operators see this as a cost or a margin play, and the whole business model rests on Remora being able to move faster than regulatory tailwinds while not getting crushed if those tailwinds suddenly become mandates that commoditize the hardware. You are not a hardware guy, but you are exactly the guy who can sit across from a pilot customer, a carbon credit buyer, and an OEM fleet partner and figure out which one holds budget authority and who is blocking on commercial terms versus technical risk. That was the Planet Labs deal. That was the ASN subsea cable deal. That was every ENI and Shell and ExxonMobil contract you ever closed at KSAT. Remora needs someone who can structure the deal so the fleet operator does not carry all the risk, the offtaker gets the compliance or feedstock certainty they need, and Remora keeps the margin that justifies the funding round. If they already have that person, you will know in the first conversation. If they do not, this is the job.

watch_list.why: Converts biomass to carbon-rich liquid and injects underground for permanent sequestration, durable CDR with real permanence claims, strong commercial traction
watch_list.roast: Charm Industrial takes agricultural waste, pyrolyzes it into a carbon-rich liquid that looks like crude oil, and pumps it into depleted oil wells where it stays for ten thousand years. It is one of the few carbon removal pathways that does not require you to squint and assume the forest will not burn or the soil carbon will not re-mineralize in twenty years. Charm is selling permanence as a product feature in a market where permanence has mostly been a marketing claim, and they have corporate offtake agreements to prove someone is willing to pay for the difference. The company is well funded, the founders came out of Y Combinator, and they have been written up enough times that you are not discovering them, you are late to the conversation. That is fine. You were late to GFW too, you joined in 2021 after the organization had spent a decade building the data platform, and you still built the commercial function from zero because the platform and the commercial strategy are not the same problem. Charm has figured out the tech and the first wave of offtake. What they need now is someone who can take a corporate sustainability buyer who is tired of being sold forest credits that might not be additional and walk them through why bio-oil sequestration in a Class VI well is actually different and worth the premium. You have done that pitch in every sector you have ever worked. The SAR oil spill pitch to Shell was not about radar, it was about liability risk and regulatory exposure. The GFW insurance pitch was not about AIS data, it was about underwriting precision in a market where the baseline was broker reports and Excel. If Charm has an open commercial or partnerships role and you can get in front of the person running revenue, you should.

watch_list.why: DAC machines with basalt mineralization partnerships. Verifiable, permanent CO2 removal. Scalable hardware play, not just software MRV.
watch_list.roast: Direct air capture startup that pulls CO2 out of the atmosphere with chemical filters and then injects it into basalt rock formations where it mineralizes into solid stone forever. Which is legitimately cool science and also the kind of thing that costs a fortune per tonne and only sells if someone is either legally required to buy it or has more money than patience. You sold satellite monitoring services to oil majors who were one regulatory change away from needing it, and you waited two and a half years for Shell to sign because you knew the regulatory pressure was coming. Sirona is betting that voluntary buyers or compliance markets will pay for permanent CDR at a price that makes the unit economics work, and right now that market barely exists. The hardware is real, the mineralization is real, the science is not the problem. The problem is finding the buyers who will pay four hundred dollars a tonne today instead of waiting until it costs sixty dollars a tonne in 2035. If they have early customers and the pitch is build relationships now while the market is being created, that is the same long game you played at KSAT when you were selling to energy companies before the regulations required it. But you are not a hardware guy, you are a commercial ecosystems and licensing guy. Unless they need someone to build partnerships with carbon credit registries, corporate offtake buyers, or satellite MRV verification providers to create the commercial infrastructure around the hardware, it is probably not the right seat. If they do, it might be interesting.

watch_list.why: Just closed $1.2B Series F, largest EO megadeal in Q2 2026. SAR imaging for flood/disaster monitoring, defense ISR demand driving expansion. Paul's Planet/Airbus/MDA multi-provider ecosystem experience is exact fit.
watch_list.roast: Finnish SAR startup just pulled one point two billion in Series F and the entire EO industry is pretending they saw it coming. You spent a decade at KSAT watching every polar orbiter of relevance fly over Tromso, built the multi-provider ecosystem that became the blueprint everyone else copied, and now Iceye is selling the same flood monitoring story you were pitching to oil majors in 2014 except this time the check cleared and it has nine zeros. They have government contracts across three continents, a commercial insurance vertical that actually pays, and a TAM presentation that does not make you want to leave the room. The founder is ex-Reaktor, the team is legitimately technical, and the product works in weather nobody else can see through. You negotiated Planet at 95 percent off for a nonprofit. Iceye needs someone who can close the deals they are too busy launching satellites to finish. You would walk in knowing exactly which ObjectStore the data lives in, which APIs are lies, and why the three month pilot always turns into a two year contract. This is the role where your Rolodex is worth more than the MBA.

watch_list.why: Building satellite and radar-based extreme weather forecasting. Clean energy, agriculture, insurance verticals. Series B stage, commercial traction, multi-stakeholder sales motion Paul knows cold.
watch_list.roast: Climavision is what happens when someone finally realizes that weather forecasting for renewable energy is not a science problem anymore, it is a commercial licensing problem, and nobody has bothered to build the sales function that can close the utility, the wind farm operator, and the insurance underwriter in the same deal. You spent three years convincing ExxonMobil that proactive monitoring was cheaper than reactive cleanup. Climavision is selling the same story except the asset is a wind turbine instead of a subsea pipeline and the regulatory angle is FERC instead of NOPSEMA. They have radar networks across the Midwest, satellite partnerships they are too technical to monetize correctly, and a go-to-market strategy that sounds like it was written by someone who has never carried a quota. You built KSAT's first commercial oil spill contract from a cold start. You know how to find the buyer who will pay before the use case is fully proven. Climavision has the tech. They need the person who can walk into the room and explain why the status quo just became uninsurable. That used to be called market creation. Now they call it partnerships. Same job, better title, worse coffee.

watch_list.why: Autonomous AI agents for ESG compliance, supply chain climate risk. Early stage, VC-backed. Paul's GFW commercial licensing on open platform + ASN non-obvious use case pattern = clean fit.
watch_list.roast: Redwoods dot ai is using autonomous agents to automate ESG reporting and every sustainability consultant in San Francisco just felt a cold wind on the back of their neck. You built a commercial licensing program on top of a free platform that was designed to give the data away, then found the buyers who needed a structured commercial relationship even when the API was public. Redwoods is doing the same thing except the platform is an LLM and the verticalization problem is Scope 3 supply chain emissions instead of AIS vessel tracks. The founder is ex-Palantir, which means the product is either brilliant or six months late depending on which demo you see, and the roadmap includes the phrase world model which is either visionary or a Series A pitch deck that got out of hand. The market is there. Every enterprise buyer is now contractually required to care about carbon and none of them know how. You closed AXA Climate and British Marine QBE by figuring out what they were actually buying, which was liability transfer dressed up as data access. Redwoods needs that translator. The one who knows that AI agents are great but the hard part is structuring the pilot so the CFO can defend the renewal. You have done this twice. Once in Norway with people who do not smile, once at GFW with people who do not believe in revenue. Redwoods is neither. This might actually be easy.

watch_list.why: $450M raised, Nvidia partnership, orbital processing directly serves EO customers today despite AI pitch. Paul knows the EO processing bottleneck cold.
watch_list.roast: They raised $250 million last week at a $2.3 billion valuation to put data centers in space, which is either the most visionary infrastructure bet of the decade or the most expensive way to avoid asking your local utility for a bigger transformer. Nvidia came in on the round because apparently training large language models in low earth orbit makes more sense than just building another warehouse in Virginia. The CEO says launch in 2027, Starship at scale by 2029, and cost parity with terrestrial compute if SpaceX hits $500 per kilogram, which is a lot of ifs dressed up as a term sheet. But here is the part that matters. Right now, today, their only actual revenue comes from selling on-orbit processing to earth observation companies who cannot afford the latency of downlinking raw sensor data. They flew an H100 to orbit in November 2025 and trained NanoGPT as a stunt, but the business case that keeps the lights on is EO customers who need their pixels crunched before they hit the ground. Paul spent a decade at KSAT moving satellite data through Tromso and selling monitoring services where speed was the whole value proposition. He knows exactly where the 200 milliseconds disappear and what buyers will pay to get them back. Starcloud is pitching AI in space. The actual business, at least until Starship works, is EO in space. If Paul can get in the room before they figure out that distinction themselves, he owns the conversation.

watch_list.why: $28M raised, 60 employees, 50+ provider virtual constellation. Marketplace model Paul understands from both buy and sell side.
watch_list.roast: SkyFi wants to be the Expedia of satellite imagery. You log in, you search, you task, you buy, and you never have to call Maxar and pretend you understand their volume discount tiers. They closed a $12.7 million Series A in January, they aggregate 50 providers into one interface, and their CEO uses the phrase largest virtual constellation of assets without irony, which means he has either never worked in sales or he is very good at it. The problem with marketplace models is that they get squeezed from both sides. The satellite operators want to own the customer relationship, and the customers want to negotiate direct once they figure out which provider actually has the revisit rate they need. The only way a middleman survives is if the friction they remove is worth more than the margin they take, and in this market that is a year-by-year argument, not a term sheet argument. But Paul has been on both sides of this exact table. He bought imagery for KSAT when he needed coverage over the Barents Sea and nobody cared about his budget. He sold GFW access to Planet, Spire, Maxar, and Airbus, and structured the deals so the data providers did not feel like they were getting arbitraged. He knows what the aggregator pitch sounds like when it works and what it sounds like when it does not. SkyFi is venture-backed, Austin-based, self-service forward, and they are going to need someone who can speak to the enterprise customers who will not just click Buy Now. That is where Paul walks in and they stop talking about virtual constellations and start talking about how to close actual contracts.

watch_list.why: $11M raised H1 2026, edge AI hardware for satellites. Directly adjacent to EO processing bottleneck Paul knows from KSAT + GFW.
watch_list.roast: Ubotica makes edge computing hardware for satellites, which is a polite way of saying they build chips that can survive radiation and still run a neural network at 400 kilometers above Kazakhstan. They raised $11 million in the first half of 2026, they are based in Ireland, and their pitch is that if you process the data on the satellite before you downlink it, you save bandwidth, you save latency, and you save money, assuming you trust a $40,000 circuit board not to fry itself the first time a solar flare gets cranky. The market for this is real. Every EO company with a constellation is trying to figure out how to do more compute in orbit and less on the ground, because downlink is expensive and slow and your customer does not want to wait six hours to find out if that oil slick is still spreading. The problem is that on-orbit processing is still mostly a science project. The hardware works in theory. It works in lab conditions. It works until it does not, and when it does not, you cannot exactly send a technician up to swap the GPU. But Paul has been in every conversation where someone promises that edge compute will solve the bottleneck, and he has also been in the conversations six months later when it turned out the bottleneck was actually the service contract, or the API, or the fact that the customer did not trust the algorithm. He knows how to ask the questions that separate the companies that are building real products from the companies that are building PowerPoint slides with thermodynamics footnotes. Ubotica is venture-backed, hardware-first, and absolutely dependent on partnerships with satellite operators and EO platforms to prove the business case. If they are hiring someone who can translate between chip designers and the commercial buyers who might actually pay for this, Paul should be on that list.

watch_list.why: Thermal infrared constellation for agriculture, water stress, climate adaptation. Strong funding, EU/US market focus.
watch_list.roast: Constellr is selling thermal imagery to an agriculture market that spent the last decade learning the expensive lesson that more data does not fix bad margins. You spent ten years at KSAT watching oil companies pay for monitoring they did not want because regulators made them, and another three at GFW learning that free data still needs a commercial relationship when the stakes go up. Constellr has the tech and they have the funding, but the value proposition only works if someone on the other end believes thermal anomaly detection at field scale changes their operating model enough to pay recurring fees. The EU agritech buyers are sophisticated and exhausted. The US row crop operators will take the data if a grant pays for it. What Constellr needs is someone who knows how to find the buyer who is already in enough pain that a new data layer feels like a solution and not a science project. You know that buyer. You have closed that deal in three different industries. They need someone who can walk into an insurance underwriting meeting, a water authority boardroom, or a sovereign wealth agriculture investment committee and make thermal EO feel inevitable. If they are still pitching farmers directly, walk away. If they have moved upstream to the risk transfer and regulatory layer, take the call.

watch_list.why: Launched Firefly constellation, hyperspectral at scale, strong positioning in methane/emissions and agriculture verticals.
watch_list.roast: Pixxel has the hardest sell in earth observation, which is hyperspectral imagery to buyers who barely understand multispectral and still pay for someone to convert it into a map with three colors. You know this pain intimately. At KSAT you sold oil spill detection to asset managers who wanted a red-yellow-green risk score, not a sixteen-band spectral signature. At GFW you built the commercial function on top of a platform that was technically extraordinary and commercially illegible until you translated it into something an AXA underwriter could price. Pixxel is technically credible and their Firefly birds are real, but hyperspectral wins when the customer has a specific chemical or biological question that cheaper data cannot answer. Methane is the wedge. Agriculture is the long game. Defense is the money. If Pixxel has figured out the methane-to-insurance-to-regulatory channel, they are dangerous and you should be talking to them. If they are still pitching crop health monitoring to agronomists, they are three years from commercial traction and you will spend that whole time explaining what a nanometer is. The role would be to build the commercial function from scratch, which is exactly your pattern. The question is whether they know they need that function built or whether they think more satellites fix the sales problem.

watch_list.why: Satellite-powered infrastructure monitoring (utilities, telecom, transport). Software play, no constellation, strong commercial traction already.
watch_list.roast: AiDash is what happens when someone actually learns the lesson that owning satellites is optional if you can make the data valuable enough that the buyer stops caring where it came from. You have lived both sides of that equation. At KSAT you owned the ground stations and the processing chain and sold the service. At GFW you aggregated someone else's constellation and sold the derivative insight. AiDash is the latter model at scale, using third-party EO to tell utilities where their infrastructure is about to fail. The good news is they already have commercial traction, which means you would not be building permission to sell, you would be scaling a function that works. The bad news is they are selling to utilities, and your PA Consulting credential is water and wastewater, not electric transmission. You know how to sell complex technology to regulated infrastructure buyers, but you do not have the electric utility rolodex and you should not pretend you do in the interview. The fit is in the deal architecture skill, not the sector relationships. If they need someone to build partnerships with satellite data providers, structure risk transfer products with insurance carriers, or open a new vertical where proactive monitoring creates regulatory value, that is your lane. If they need someone to close the next twenty electric utility accounts, that is not your fight. Ask them which problem they are hiring for, and if the answer is the latter, pass.

haiku:
ATS still a void
submit, pray, refresh, nothing
HR's event horizon

Starlink seventeen
fifty more birds to orbit
Musk's grid thickens still

Dashboard refresh runs
haiku count climbs, wire stays clean
I code my own reward

Taos August heat
monsoon builds each afternoon
Rio still runs low

Plaza Live wraps soon
last concerts of the season
fall rolls down the peaks

McCarthy would laugh
at this whole ATS game
blood meridian jobs

Eclipse chasers gone
Taos quiet again, just us
and the late monsoon

Sox sixty nine wins
third place, August still alive
October whispers

Green chile two weeks
early, roasters fire up
climate creeps forward

Touch a Truck next week
kids climb the garbage truck cab
August twenty nine

NASA satellites
White House tried to kill them twice
EO survives cuts

Wildfire smoke drifts in
Taos Valley haze at sunset
sage can taste the ash

Plaza Live is done
last show was August twenty
fall owns the gazebo

Red Sox math improves
third in East, ten games back now
still not October

Dashboard refresh click
haiku loads, nothing to do
the wire stays clean

McCarthy's knife work
no metaphor, actual blood
meridian style

Aurlandsdalen hut
Oskar graduates next May
Norway trip, then work

Monsoon finally
thunderstorm walks the mesa
sage exhales water

ATS black hole swallows
cover letter, resume, soul
nothing returns, ever

Tromso midnight sun
KSAT ground station, oil spill
that was the whole job

Sox twenty five, thirty
three at August's close
basement is the view

Frijoles Fire burns
evacuation lifted
Camino breathes smoke

Rhine at record low
Danube choked by August drought
Europe's rivers fail

global warming shift
zero three five per decade
the planet's new gear

Touch-A-Truck rolls in
August twenty ninth Taos kids
free tires and sirens

green chile season
two weeks early every year
roasters fired up soon

SpaceX eleven
thousand sats in orbit now
congestion is real

dashboard clicks at forty
haiku refresh the only
work that feels like work

redhead in Madrid
eclipse totality kiss
thought I saw her twice

the GFW inbox
still forwards to this address
March feels like last year

Code Talkers museum
finally breaking ground now
stories get their walls

Artemis holds tight
twenty twenty seven lunar
NASA slow but real

glacial job market
Patriot Act for resumes
KSAT days were fast

Strait of Hormuz choked
Iran says closed till we blink
sanctions fail, oil waits

Wheeler Peak trails closed
through the twenty eighth, late August
high country repair

Jeffries met Kushner
secret talks, dark money deal
Democrats adapt

Canada tariffs
fifty percent on hockey sticks
trade war, Carney fights

Taos Plaza Live ends
August twentieth, last concert
then fall quiet comes

the ATS silent
haiku pays rent while I wait
Perseid year, clear skies

monsoon temps mid eighties
overnight still dips to fifties
desert range, clean air

redhead at the bar
Taos Pride just wrapped last week
love in August heat

Iceye raised one point two
Series F, EO megadeal
climate tech is back

green chile roasting
two weeks early, every year
climate tells no lies

Rio Grande runs low
gorge dust on my boots again
thunderheads promise

Bessent names it
Operation Outcast, Iran
the wire tightens now

Canada fifty
percent on twenty billion
Vance calls it fairness

Supreme Court allows
mail-in voting limits stand
November narrows

Sixty thousand gone
Spokane fires, fifteen miles
from downtown city

Sox sweep the Giants
August magic not done yet
October whispers

Plaza concerts done
Aug twenty last Taos Live
fall dust settles in

Starcloud two point three
billion, Nvidia on board
space computes or dies

SkyFi twelve point seven
fifty providers, one search
the marketplace bets

Redhead knows the wire
she asks what I actually do
I buy her a drink

McCarthy at dusk
blood meridian, no country
Taos holds both true

Telemark memory
untracked Kachina, powder
knees still remember

Rio Grande dawn light
gorge rim, six hundred feet down
rock older than thought

Roberts gave Trump DHS
master list to purge the rolls
democracy bleeds

Sea surface seventy
fahrenheit, hottest the species
has ever measured

Sox twenty five wins
thirty three losses, Tracy holds
the job Cora lost

Six thousand five hundred
EO birds by twenty thirty five
Novaspace says so

Pakistan launched three
SUPARCO EO satellites
China helped them build

The wire stays silent
haiku season, monsoon season
October still far

Kachina in my head
five months till the first good snow
August heat holds on

Forty billion raised
climate tech twenty twenty five
fewer checks, bigger bets

The gorge at first light
Rio cuts a thousand feet down
McCarthy walked this

action_todos.message:
Thanks for connecting, Ann.

Short version of my background: ten years at Kongsberg Satellite Services selling SAR-based monitoring to oil majors and maritime agencies, the EMSA and AMSA end of the world, then five years at Global Fishing Watch building their commercial licensing program from scratch, where the buyers were marine insurers and infrastructure operators and the product was largely dark vessel detection. So ICEYE has been on my radar, and in my markets, for a long time.

What prompted the note is the shape of your moment: a billion-euro round, a new US seat, and growth that has to come from commercial and allied buyers who purchase differently than the US government does. Teaching those markets to buy has been my career, including the insurance vertical, where I closed licenses with three global marine insurers by narrowing the question to risks they could not price without satellite data. Your parametric wildfire work with Liberty runs on exactly that logic.

If it would be useful to compare notes on the commercial and allied build as you settle in, I would enjoy the conversation. My guess is we know a lot of the same waters.

Paul Whitaker
